name: TPS78233DDCR
title: 150 mA LDO regulator with 500 nA quiescent current
summary: TPS782 is a family of fixed-output 150 mA LDO regulators that draw 0.42 µA typical ground current at no load and 18 nA in shutdown, for battery-powered microcontroller systems. Input runs from 2.2 V to 5.5 V; outputs from 1.8 V to 3.6 V are set at the factory. A PMOS pass device gives 130 mV typical dropout at 150 mA, and a 1 µF ceramic output capacitor keeps it stable. It has an active-high CMOS enable, current limit, thermal shutdown and an active output discharge, in a TSOT23-5 (DDC) or 2 mm x 2 mm SON-6 (DRV) package.

circuits.description: The regulator with only its two capacitors: the supply enters IN with a 1 µF capacitor to ground, the fixed output leaves OUT with a 1 µF capacitor to ground, and EN takes an on/off control. The output voltage is set by which TPS782xx is fitted.

equations.name: Output discharge time
equations.expr: t = 3 × (10 kΩ × RL) / (10 kΩ + RL) × COUT

where.t: time for the output to fall to within 5% of VOUT after shutdown

where.PD: power dissipated in the pass element

operation.text: A fixed-output LDO built round a PMOS pass device, aimed at battery products where standby current matters: ground current is 0.42 µA typical with no load. Inside are a bandgap reference driven from EN, current limit, thermal shutdown, an EPROM and multiplexer that set the output voltage at the factory, logic, and an active pulldown of 10 kΩ on OUT. Any output capacitance over 1.0 µF keeps it stable, and with no load at all; EN accepts standard CMOS levels and suits MSP430 systems.

In overload the output supplies a roughly fixed current whatever the output voltage; the part should not be left in current limit for long. The pass device's body diode conducts from OUT to IN whenever OUT is higher than IN, and that current is not limited; if reverse voltage may last, an external limit of about 5% of the rated output current may be needed.
When the regulator is off, an internal pulldown discharges OUT, provided the input is above 2.2 V. Discharge time to within 5% of VOUT follows the discharge-time equation.

EN turns the part on when high and accepts both ordinary and low-voltage CMOS logic; above 1.2 V the part runs and below 0.4 V it shuts down. Where shutdown is not needed EN is wired to IN. EN must never exceed VIN + 0.3 V, during start-up or in steady state.

Normal regulation needs VIN above VOUT(nom) + VDO, EN to have risen past its rising threshold and not since fallen below its falling threshold, load under the current limit and the die below the thermal shutdown point. With input below VOUT(nom) + VDO the part is in dropout: the output follows the input, the pass transistor sits in triode and no longer regulates, and line or load steps can move the output a long way. EN below its falling threshold (or never having passed the rising one), or the die above the shutdown temperature, disables the part.

No input capacitor is needed for stability, but 0.1 µF to 1.0 µF of low-ESR capacitance near the part offsets reactive sources and gives better step response, noise and ripple rejection; more is needed for large fast load steps or a distant source, and 0.1 µF may be needed for stability when the source impedance is high. On the output, ceramic capacitors of 1.0 µF or more are stable; X5R and X7R are preferred for their small change over temperature, ESR must be below 1.0 Ω, and after tolerance and DC bias at least 1 µF must remain. A larger output capacitor gives less over- and undershoot but a longer transient.

Below the dropout voltage the PMOS transistor works in its linear region and IN to OUT is just its on-resistance, so dropout rises roughly in proportion to load current. PSRR and transient response worsen as VIN - VOUT nears dropout.
A dedicated low-current circuit keeps the loop regulating at very light load, so the part is stable and holds regulation all the way to no load.
Choose the part number for the output voltage needed; the supply must cover dropout headroom and carry the load current plus ground pin current.

A 1 µF or larger ceramic capacitor sits right at OUT and no further than 10 mm away; 0.1 µF to 1.0 µF of low-ESR capacitance goes between IN and GND. The supply should have low output impedance and connect directly to IN; inductance between source and IN causes large voltage swings at IN during start-up and load steps, and an input capacitor is then needed.

For best PSRR, noise and transient response, the input and output sides get separate ground planes that join only at the device GND pin, and the output capacitor's ground runs straight to that pin. High-ESR capacitors can reduce PSRR. In the DDC layout example CIN sits beside pin 1 and COUT beside pin 5 over a ground plane.

The output switches off when the junction reaches about 160°C and back on once it cools to about 140°C, so with sustained overload the part cycles. Junction temperature should be kept at or below 125°C; to check margin, raise ambient with worst-case load until protection trips, which should not happen until ambient is 35°C or more above the highest expected. Running repeatedly into thermal shutdown reduces reliability.

Heat leaves through the board: clear copper area round the part, heavier copper and plated vias into heat-spreading layers all help. Dissipation is the load current times the input-to-output drop. On the DRV package the exposed pad is soldered down to the board.
